Article Text:

Former England captain Ben Stokes could emerge as the costliest buy at the upcoming IPL mini-auction, scheduled to be held in Goa on December 16. The 35-year-old is listed at the highest base price of Rs 2 crore.Stokes, who has represented three IPL franchises in the past, is expected to trigger a bidding war between Lucknow Super Giants (LSG) and Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR). The two franchises will enter the mini-auction with purses of Rs 47.45 crore and Rs 41.65 crore, respectively.In 2017, Stokes was the most expensive overseas player at the auction when he was bought for Rs 14.5 crore by the then Sanjiv Goenka-owned Pune franchise. The all-rounder scored 316 runs and picked up 12 wickets in 12 outings. Now, with LSG looking for a captain and someone who can provide stability in the middle order while also delivering four overs, Stokes could prove to be a gold-dust acquisition.In Aiden Markram, Mitchell Marsh and Nicholas Pooran, LSG have a power-packed top order but a relatively fragile middle order. They have already acquired Sam Curran in a trade from the Rajasthan Royals, but will still be looking for a captain.Since reaching the IPL playoffs in 2022 and 2023, LSG have finished seventh in 2024 and 2025, before improving a touch to fifth in 2026.Meanwhile, KKR, after releasing their captain Ajinkya Rahane, will also enter the mini-auction hoping to find a leader. The franchise has released 12 players, including four overseas and eight Indian players.With Stokes now retired from international cricket and available for the entire IPL season, landing him could be a significant boost for either franchise. His presence could immediately strengthen their title ambitions and give them a player around whom the next cycle (2026-30) could be built.The 35-year-old has not played a T20 since the 2024 edition of The Hundred, where he picked up a hamstring injury. He was due to appear in the SA20 for MI Cape Town in early 2025 but was ruled out after another hamstring injury.Unlike his ex-England teammate Harry Brook -- who is serving a two-season ban for withdrawing before the tournament began -- Stokes has safely entered the mini-auction.Stokes, who has played for Rising Pune Supergiant, Rajasthan Royals and Chennai Super Kings in the IPL, didn't enter the 2025 mega auction. According to the rules, he was ineligible for the 2026 season but can, and has, enter the 2027 mini-auction.After retiring from international cricket in June, Stokes returned to playing for Durham and helped them secure promotion to Division One of the County Championship. However, he has hinted that he could miss at least the first six rounds of County matches if he is picked at the IPL mini-auction.Stokes has played 45 matches in the IPL and has amassed 935 runs, including two hundreds. With the ball, he's taken 28 wickets.
Article Summary: Former England captain Ben Stokes could emerge as the costliest buy at the upcoming IPL mini-auction. The 35-year-old is listed at the highest base price of Rs 2 crore. Stokes is expected to trigger a bidding war between Lucknow Super Giants (LSG) and Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR)

Article Title: '28-ball hundred to double ton': Tilak Varma stunned by Sooryavanshi's record-breaking 204, explains Pakistan loss comments
Article Text:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and Tilak Varma

Sooryavanshi turns the game into a six-hitting spectacle

Tilak explains comments after Pakistan defeat

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India A captain Tilak Varma was left amazed by Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's extraordinary 53-ball 204 against the UAE in the Rising Stars Asia Cup, admitting that even the team did not expect the 15-year-old to produce such a breathtaking performance.Sooryavanshi smashed the fastest List A century, reaching the milestone in just 28 balls, before completing his double hundred off 52 deliveries. His innings, which included a staggering 28 sixes, powered India A to a seven-wicket victory as they chased down 250 in just 14.2 overs in their Group B encounter on Tuesday."It was an absolutely fantastic innings to watch. A 28-ball hundred is something! Everyone knows that he will break the record, but we haven't thought that he will break it in this match only. Credit goes to him. From 28-ball hundred to double ton, it was tremendous to watch," Tilak said.The India A captain also offered an amusing insight into how the team reacts to Sooryavanshi's extraordinary hitting, revealing that the youngster is encouraged to play his natural game without worrying about taking singles."Hum usko kuch bolte nahi hai. Usse na niche se single lena nahi aata, usko hum bolte hai bhai tera jo game hi khel.Hum uska chauka celebrate nahi kar rahe the, aur 6 gaye toh hum puchte hai door gaye ki nahi? 30 sixes yaar, soch..180 runs toh uska udhar hi ho gaya," he said.Having fallen cheaply in his first two outings, Sooryavanshi made up for those disappointments in spectacular fashion, taking apart the UAE bowling attack with an astonishing display of power-hitting.The left-hander reached his first hundred off 28 balls and needed just another 24 deliveries for his second hundred. He bettered Jake Fraser-McGurk's record for the fastest List A century by a ball and comfortably surpassed Chad Bowes' 103-ball double hundred for Canterbury.His 28 sixes were the most in a single innings in professional cricket, while India A completed the chase in just 14.2 overs after UAE had posted 249/8, with Harpreet Singh Bhatia top-scoring with 130.Tilak also clarified his post-match remarks following India A's 48-run defeat against Pakistan A, which attracted criticism from sections of fans.The India A skipper had scored 100 off 149 balls in the 314-run chase but felt the team could have won had another batter stayed with him longer. Explaining his approach, he said the regular fall of wickets and the changing nature of the pitch had forced him to bat deep rather than attack from the outset."I always say, I am players' captain. In my perspective, we lost Vaibhav early then we had a partnership with Abhishek, then we lost wickets at regular intervals and we were 6 wickets down in no time. I could also start hitting from the first ball, but at that time the pitch was getting difficult," he said after the UAE game.Tilak also praised Shahbaz Ahmed, whose 56 helped him stitch together a 112-run seventh-wicket partnership."No one had thought that Shehbaz will come and start playing like that, it was a fantastic knock. I even told him in the dressing room that he won my heart with the knock. Unfortunately he got out, otherwise he would have finished the game for us," he said.The captain insisted that his comments were intended to explain the team's batting approach and not single out anyone for the defeat."I told the team after the match that one game won't define us and everyone in our team is a match-winner. My team knows I backed the team, outside noise don't bother me much," he added.
Article Summary: India A captain Tilak Varma was left amazed by Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's extraordinary 53-ball 204 against the UAE. The 15-year-old smashed the fastest List A century, reaching the milestone in just 28 balls, before completing his double hundred off 52 deliveries. His innings, which included a staggering 28 sixes, powered India A to a seven-wicket victory.

Article Title: 'It's a rich man's sport': Jeet Jhabakh opens up on the financial challenges facing Indian motorsport
Article Text:
Jeet Jhabakh

From cricket to cars: How Jeet Jhabakh found his calling

The expensive reality of motorsport in India

'Indian drivers have the talent': What separates India from Europe?

Can Formula One's return change the fortunes of Indian motorsport ?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Hyderabad-based racer Jeet Jhabakh, alongside co-driver Musa Sherif, recently won the 2026 FIA Asia-Pacific Rally Championship (APRC), becoming the first driver in the championship's 38-year history to win the overall title in a two-wheel-drive car. The duo also created history as the first all-Indian driver and co-driver pairing to clinch the continental championship.For Jeet , however, the victory is more than a personal milestone. He hopes it will open doors for Indian racers who have the talent but struggle to find the financial backing and international exposure needed to compete at the highest level.Unlike cricket, where a bat and ball can provide the starting point for a young player, motorsport requires access to specialised equipment, vehicles, training and technical support, with the costs increasing significantly as drivers move up the competitive ladder."It is an extremely expensive sport. In cricket, most people just require a bat and a ball to play. But in motorsport, you require a full-fledged car, and as you go higher and higher, the car gets more expensive. It is definitely a rich man's sport," Jeet told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive conversation.Like many Indian children, Jeet grew up playing cricket, but his interest gradually shifted towards cars as he began following Formula One and the World Rally Championship (WRC).With his family already involved in the automobile business, the transition into motorsport came naturally."Honestly, just like every other child in India, I also first started with cricket. We all could have fun playing cricket in the streets next to our houses. The first sport you tend to gravitate towards is basically a sport which is very accessible," Jeet said."As I grew older, I started watching a lot of Formula One and WRC. That's when I realised my heart had always been in cars. Fortunately, my family business is also related to cars, so it kind of tied in well with me. When I got an opportunity to get into motorsport, I jumped at it. There was no looking back at all."Despite eventually finding success in rallying, Jeet's childhood motorsport inspiration came from Formula One legend Michael Schumacher. He admired the German's dominance but was equally impressed by his race intelligence, strategy and ability to look beyond outright speed, something he has come to appreciate in his own racing career."Michael Schumacher was the person we used to really follow back in the day. He was absolutely dominant. Even though he might not have been the absolute fastest on track, his strategies and thinking were always on point," Jeet said."I always wondered whether speed was the only reason you win or whether it was a holistic approach. Now I have realised it is the holistic approach. It's not pure speed always. You have to think out of the box and be able to adapt."Jeet's experience in both circuit racing and rallying has also given him an understanding of the different skill sets the two disciplines demand.Unlike circuit racing, where drivers compete against each other on a fixed track, rallying is a race against the clock across a series of timed stages conducted on different surfaces, including gravel, dirt, tarmac and snow. Drivers are guided by their co-drivers, who read out pace notes describing upcoming corners, jumps and road conditions."In racing, you start together and compete with another person. You're fighting for that tenth of a second, pushing really hard. But in rallying, you don't compete with each other at the same point in time. There's a gap between the car in front of you and the car behind you," he explained."You tend to stick to your notes, do your best and hope that your time is better than the others. Both disciplines require different sets of skills, but they tie together in their own way."India has produced several prominent rally drivers over the years, including five-time national rally champion Hari Singh, seven-time national champion Naren Kumar and Gaurav Gill, who in 2013 became the first Indian to win the overall Asia-Pacific Rally Championship title.But for many aspiring Indian racers, securing the financial backing needed to build a career in motorsport remains one of the biggest challenges, something Jeet acknowledges from his own experience.Having never participated in competitive karting, Jeet began his competitive career through a single-make championship. His victories in the series helped him secure a sponsored drive and eventually become a factory driver for Utsavya Motorsports in 2019, an opportunity that allowed him to continue racing without having to carry the entire financial burden himself."After I won it again in 2019, I became the factory driver for Utsavya Motorsports. I was sponsored completely by them. Because of that, I got an opportunity to drive for four and a half years. I was very fortunate. A lot of people, unfortunately, don't get that opportunity," Jeet said.Beyond the cost of competing, Jeet believes one of the biggest differences between Indian drivers and their European counterparts is the amount of time they are able to dedicate to the sport.While drivers in more established motorsport ecosystems have greater opportunities to pursue racing as a full-time professional career, many Indian drivers have to balance their sporting ambitions with regular employment to finance their careers."In India, I cannot make this my only source of income because it gets very difficult. We are all working something or the other. Monday to Friday, we are working hard to make a little bit of money for ourselves to spend on racing and rallying," he explained."Over there, they are able to take this as a professional career. They are driving Monday to Friday and competing on Saturday and Sunday. With that amount of time in the car, training and guidance, there is bound to be a difference in quality over time."His own APRC victory, he feels, is evidence that Indian drivers can compete at the international level if provided with similar opportunities."If we get the same opportunity, I personally feel Indian drivers can get to that level in due course of time. I think we can compete in it. This championship is a testament that it is possible," he said.India's stint as a Formula One host between 2011 and 2013 introduced a generation of fans to international circuit racing. However, the departure of the Indian Grand Prix left a gap in the country's motorsport calendar and limited opportunities for fans to experience the sport at the highest level.For Jeet, who grew up watching Formula One and dreaming of being part of its ecosystem, the departure was particularly disappointing."Honestly, it broke my heart as a kid when Formula One decided to pull out of India. Every child who is into cars, the first thing is that you want to be a part of the whole system. When it pulled out, I was just like, man, I wish it continued," he recalled.Jeet believes the return of major international racing events, alongside the growth of domestic competitions such as the Indian Racing Festival, could help attract new fans, encourage corporate investment and create better opportunities for Indian racers."Even small races like the Indian Racing Festival coming back to India is a massive opportunity. You get to see the tracks and fast cars. That's when the public gets to know that something like this can happen," he said."A lot of media today covers sports like cricket. Badminton is also getting a lot more attention, but motorsport, even our national championships, are not really covered in the media. When something like Formula One or WRC comes to India and there is a lot of media presence, people will start getting involved.When people start watching it, more money flows into it through advertisements and sponsorships."For now, Jeet hopes his APRC triumph will encourage more businesses to invest in Indian motorsport and provide upcoming drivers with the kind of opportunities he was fortunate enough to receive early in his career."I'm hoping that this championship we've won will open doors for a lot of sponsorship, not just for myself, but for a lot of people in the country as well. There is a lot of talent here in India. Why don't we set up something in India for upcoming drivers?" he said.
Article Summary: Jeet Jhabakh won the 2026 FIA Asia-Pacific Rally Championship with co-driver Musa Sherif. He is the first driver in the championship's 38-year history to win the overall title in a two-wheel-drive car. He hopes it will open doors for Indian racers who have the talent but struggle to find the financial backing.

Vaibhav Sooryavanshi became the youngest to score a double century in all List A cricket,

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's batting impresses you the most? Power hitting Technique Biomechanics Consistency 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is explosive, yet his movements are remarkably minimal. Few batters have dismantled back-of-a-length and length deliveries down the ground with the kind of authority he has displayed over the last 18 months. He doesn't need a big stride or elaborate trigger movements to generate extraordinary power. Sometimes, all it takes is a shift in weight and those long levers.On Tuesday, the last ball of the 10th over between India A and UAE in the Asia Cup Rising Stars, when he brought up his 150 off just 40 balls, was perhaps the shot of the match. UAE pacer Zahid Ali bowled wide of the off stump, almost on the eighth-stump line. Sooryavanshi, with his long levers, transferred his weight onto the front foot and launched it over deep extra cover for six. A ball that was meant to keep him quiet was sent soaring into the stands.In recent months, Sooryavanshi has left everyone scrambling for superlatives. But Bihar coach Ashok Kumar, who has worked closely with the teenager alongside Manish Ojha, believes the bigger picture is still waiting to unfold.(He is a big fish in a small pond)," Ashok told TimesofIndia.com.(He belongs to the ocean; currently, he is in a small pond)."Following Virat Kohli’s unbeaten 82 off 51 balls against Australia during the 2016 World T20, Australian cricket writer Gideon Haigh summed up the masterclass with a memorable line in *The Australian*: “Much as the marketers would like to take the cricket out of T20, Kohli keeps putting it back.”Even in T20 cricket, the Kohli-esque style of batting was needed. It survived and thrived despite the 360-degree batting of exemplary players such as AB de Villiers and Suryakumar Yadav.But on Tuesday, the way 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi batted, it looked to be a case of putting the T20 into an ODI, almost video game-esque. At his age, kids do spend a lot of time in front of screens. Vaibhav, however, was tearing helpless UAE bowlers apart in Doha."People complain that there are too many sixes and boundaries and that the grounds are too small. But the reality is that batting has evolved massively, and it continues to evolve very quickly. Batters are now hitting length balls. The only delivery you can't really hit is a yorker," power-hitting coach Julian Wood told this website."If you look at Vaibhav's boundary-hitting patterns, he hits all around the ground, from mid-off all the way around to fine leg. If you're going to bowl wide to him, you'd probably have to bowl wide and full. But you have to execute that delivery perfectly. The problem for bowlers is that when they miss, the ball doesn't just go for four; it goes for six. That puts them under tremendous pressure."Look at Vaibhav in the IPL . He hit Jasprit Bumrah for six off the first ball and also hit Pat Cummins for six. It's almost as if there's a lack of respect, but he knows that if the bowler misses, he can hit him for six. The mindsets of both batters and bowlers have changed. Batters now think, 'If he misses, I'm going to hit him for six,'" explained Wood.Zubin Bharucha, one of Sooryavanshi’s mentors, has explained how the teenager manages to hit length deliveries with extraordinary power. He attributes it to Sooryavanshi’s coiled upper body, deep torso bend and weight-loaded back leg, which allow him to get his head outside the line of the ball and bring deliveries outside off stump directly into his eyeline."What enables him to achieve this is a superbly coiled upper half, combined with a considerable bend in his torso at the top of his swing. This allows his head to get outside the line of most deliveries," Bharucha explained.With almost all his weight loaded onto the back leg, Sooryavanshi limits forward movement of his hips and avoids the conventional transfer of weight onto the front foot. His front foot often moves only marginally, remaining relatively unloaded, which allows him to finish shots with his foot flared open and ankle turned over."He is effectively operating on one leg, which in itself suggests the weight has to remain back," Bharucha said, explaining why Sooryavanshi can generate power without committing his weight forward.The technique also allows Sooryavanshi to keep his body inside the line of the ball while his hands and bat operate in front of the stumps, a trait Bharucha compares with former greats Don Bradman and Graeme Pollock."This is driven by the deep bend in his back, which allows his hands to operate in front of the stumps, much like some of the greats of the past. They would stand well outside leg stump to ensure the bat operated in front of the stumps while the body remained well inside the line. This resulted in Bradman being dismissed LBW fewer than 10 times in his entire career, while players like Graeme Pollock never got out LBW at all. The deep bend in Sooryavanshi’s back accentuates this trait. Even though he doesn't take an outside-leg-stump guard, he is still able to achieve positions on the crease similar to those of these former greats," he said."It is all driven by the hip not sliding forward, and this enables him to remain in such a strong coiled position on one leg, from which he can create that hip-and-shoulder separation and attack every ball," he added.Bharucha believes this allows Sooryavanshi to avoid committing early to a particular length and instead turn almost every delivery into a scoring opportunity.Earlier this year, after the second IPL playoff between Rajasthan Royals and Gujarat Titans in Chandigarh, Shubman Gill had called Sooryavanshi the "best T20 batter" in the world and explained how blessed the teenager was with his biomechanics."I've not seen anyone bat like the way he bats, and I think in this format, he's right now one of the best batters in the world. It is just not his hitting, but his biomechanics and his hand speed, and, you know, no matter what opposition he plays against. I think, in the years to come, the opposition that he plays against is going to have a tough time against him," he had said.Meanwhile, Julian Wood compares his bat swing with that of a baseball player."If you look at Vaibhav, the way his hands come up is very much like a baseball batter. His bat goes past the perpendicular, which is something you wouldn't necessarily coach. But he can generate serious bat speed. Because his bat goes further past the perpendicular, he has more room to whip his hands through the ball and generate speed," he said.With his 53-ball 204 against the UAE, Sooryavanshi has rewritten the record books in spectacular fashion. Currently, he is not even a regular in T20Is, but he certainly is a big fish in a small pond. He should be thrown into the deep sea. And with age on his side, just imagine how many remarkable things he can do with his bat.
Article Summary: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi scored a a 53-ball 204 against UAE. The 15-year-old became the youngest to score a double century in all List A cricket. He now owns the record for the fastest 50, 100, 150 and 200 in List A.

Article Title: 'Ridiculous stage white-ball cricket has reached': Sanjay Manjrekar raises concern after Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's 204
Article Text:
Sanjay Manjrekar Questions State Of White-Ball Cricket

Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's record-breaking 204 against UAE

Former India batter Sanjay Manjrekar has heaped praise on teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi following his extraordinary batting display against the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in the Rising Stars Asia Cup 2026. However, while acknowledging the youngster's exceptional talent, Manjrekar also raised concerns over the growing imbalance between bat and ball in white-ball cricket.Sooryavanshi produced a record-breaking performance in Doha on Tuesday, smashing a sensational 204 off just 53 deliveries to help India A chase down a target of 250 in only 14.2 overs. His innings featured seven boundaries and a staggering 28 sixes, making it one of the most remarkable knocks in List A cricket.Reacting to the teenager's extraordinary display, Manjrekar took to X and questioned whether the current direction of white-ball cricket was genuinely what fans wanted to see."There is something special about Vaibhav no doubt about that. But what he did is another reminder of the ridiculous stage white ball cricket has reached. It's a fallacy to think that this is what fans want. It's a game of bat & ball. Not just bat," Manjrekar wrote.The 15-year-old left-hander unleashed a stunning assault on the UAE bowling attack, reaching his century in just 28 balls to register the fastest hundred in List A cricket. He went on to complete his 150 in 40 deliveries before bringing up his double century off just 52 balls.In the process, Sooryavanshi broke several records, including the previous fastest List A century held by Australia's Jake Fraser-McGurk, who had reached the milestone in 29 balls.His 28 sixes were also the most by a batter in a single innings in professional cricket. He finished with a strike rate of 384.90, setting another List A record for the highest strike rate in an innings of 100 or more runs.India A eventually reached 254/3 in just 14.2 overs to register a seven-wicket victory, chasing down the UAE's total of 249/8 with 214 balls to spare.
Article Summary: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi produced a record-breaking performance in Doha on Tuesday. The 15-year-old smashed a sensational 204 off just 53 deliveries to help India A chase down a target of 250 in only 14.2 overs. His innings featured seven boundaries and a staggering 28 sixes, making it one of the most remarkable knocks in List A cricket. Former India batter Sanjay Manjrekar has heaped praise on the teenager.

Article Title: Punjab Kings appoint Paras Mhambrey as fast bowling coach ahead of IPL 2027
Article Text:
Paras Mhambrey

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Punjab Kings (PBKS) have appointed Paras Mhambrey as their fast bowling coach ahead of IPL 2027, the franchise announced on Wednesday.Mhambrey's appointment comes after PBKS parted ways with bowling coach James Hopes and fielding coach Brad Haddin last month. He will work under head coach Ricky Ponting , having previously been part of the Australian's coaching setup at Mumbai Indians.Mhambrey was India's bowling coach under Rahul Dravid from 2021 to 2024. During this period, he was part of the coaching staff that guided India to the 2023 ODI World Cup final at home and the 2024 T20 World Cup title in the Caribbean.He has also worked with Mumbai Indians in two stints. Mhambrey returned to the franchise after his time with the Indian team but left last month following a restructuring of its coaching staff.PBKS are yet to win an IPL title, having finished runners-up twice. They lost the 2014 final to Kolkata Knight Riders before going down to Royal Challengers Bengaluru in 2025.The franchise had a strong start to IPL 2026, winning six of its first seven matches, while the other game was washed out. However, PBKS could not maintain that run in the second half of the league stage. They managed only one more win in their remaining seven matches and failed to qualify for the playoffs.Led by India T20I captain Shreyas Iyer, PBKS will enter the December 16 auction in Goa with 19 players retained. They have a purse of Rs 18.60 crore and six slots to fill, including two for overseas players.
Article Summary: Paras Mhambrey has been appointed fast bowling coach for Punjab Kings. He will work under head coach Ricky Ponting. PBKS parted ways with bowling coach James Hopes and fielding coach Brad Haddin last month. They are yet to win an IPL title, having finished runners-up twice.

Article Title: 'Time to hang them up': Stuart MacGill tells Nathan Lyon to make way for Australia's next generation of spinners
Article Text:
Australia's Nathan Lyon (Reuters Photo)

MacGill wants opportunities for younger spinners

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

O'Keefe backs Lyon for India tour

Former Australia leg-spinner Stuart MacGill believes Nathan Lyon 's time in the Test side is up, going a step further by suggesting the veteran should consider retiring from first-class cricket to make way for younger spinners chasing international ambitions.MacGill believes the 39-year-old is occupying a place that could be better utilised by emerging talent, both at the national and state levels, and has questioned whether Lyon still merits a place in Australia's plans."I've been of this mind for quite some time - nothing personal against Nathan, but I just think that he's just holding a place at the moment," MacGill said on the Chin Music podcast. "I'll go as far as to say I think he's a placeholder in the NSW team as well."Lyon has come under increasing scrutiny following Australia's recent tour of South Africa, where he was left out of the second Test in Gqeberha before managing just four wickets in 67 overs in the third Test in Cape Town. South African spinner Simon Harmer , meanwhile, claimed 10 wickets in the match.MacGill believes Lyon's continued presence in the New South Wales side is restricting opportunities for 24-year-old Tanveer Sangha, who has represented Australia in white-ball cricket but is looking to establish himself in the longer format."I'm not sure whether or not now is the right time for him to go 'You know what? I've been a great bowler for Australia, I've taken a lot of wickets for Australia and the various states that I've played for, but maybe it's time to hang them up'," he said."I'd just like to see some other guys get opportunities for NSW. If he's not in the Australian team, he's keeping guys like Tanveer (Sangha) out of the NSW team, which is a shame," the 55-year-old added.MacGill also questioned the need to carry Lyon in the squad when Australia already have other spin options, including Matt Kuhnemann and Cooper Connolly, as well as former New Zealand captain and spin great Daniel Vettori on the coaching staff."You've got Dan Vettori as part of that group. I don't think you need to take up one of the playing spots with a guy that's not going to play," he said. "You've got Kuhnemann, Connolly..."Fellow former Australia spinner Steve O'Keefe disagreed with MacGill, arguing that Lyon's experience could prove invaluable during Australia's upcoming five-Test tour of India. However, he acknowledged that the veteran's place should not be taken for granted."I'd like to keep Nathan Lyon in the team, and this is one of the main reasons: they're going to go to India, and I think having an experienced spinner there for five Tests will be really important," O'Keefe said.Lyon has taken 577 wickets in 145 Tests, making him Australia's second-highest wicket-taker in the format. Australia are scheduled to announce their squad for the four-Test series against New Zealand, beginning December 9, after the ongoing Sheffield Shield round.
Article Summary: Former Australia leg-spinner Stuart MacGill believes Nathan Lyon's time in the Test side is up. The 39-year-old should retire from first-class cricket to make way for younger spinners chasing international ambitions, says the former spinner. Lyon has come under increasing scrutiny following Australia's recent tour of South Africa, where he was left out of the second Test.

Article Title: NorthEast United, SC Delhi share spoils on ISL’s debut in Imphal
Article Text:
Antonio Moyano (Pic credit: NEUFC)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Manipur fans were treated to some end-to-end football as NorthEast United FC and SC Delhi played out an exciting 1-1 draw on Indian Super League ’s debut in the football-loving state.The sharing of honours at the sold-out Khuman Lampak Stadium in Imphal meant that there was no change in their positions in the table as NEUFC stayed in third spot, with 12 points from seven matches, while SC Delhi were still a rung below with nine points from their seven games. To the surprise of the fans who packed Khuman Lampak on a chilly Tuesday evening, carrying banners and wearing the jerseys of the club from their region, the visitors began the match with gusto and created one attack after another in NEUFC half.And it did not take them long to convert one of the opportunities, courtesy of the skills of Mohammed Aimen in front of goal in the sixth minute. Receiving the ball after a rebound just outside the box, the 23-year-old cut in between two NEUFC defenders and curled in a brilliant shot that beat the leaping Gurmeet Singh and swerved into the right corner.Delhi could have increased their lead soon after as Aimen was exceptional down the left and near the goal, to the disappointment of the Imphal crowd.Even as NEUFC tried to press for an equaliser, Nduka Junior and Ashutosh Mehta kept on doggedly guarding the Delhi defence.But the packed house in the Manipur capital came alive in the 29th minute as a chip from Nikhil Barla from outside the box, perfectly timed, left the until-then solid Delhi defence ball-watching.Moyano took time to receive the ball in front of an open goal and left goalkeeper Nora Fernandez with no chance as his shot thumped into the left corner of the goal.It was their ninth goal from open play this season and made the cheers around the venue even louder.The equaliser slowed down the pace of the game as Delhi tried to regroup while not letting NEUFC take advantage of their new-found confidence. While there were a few half-chances for the Highlanders, the game stayed level at half-time.Delhi seemed to have regained their lead soon after the change of ends as Lalrinliana Hnamte was declared offside by the assistant moments after the referee had deemed his shot a goal. The frustrated Delhi head coach Tomasz Tchorz was shown a yellow card as he protested that Hnamte had been onside when the last touch was made by Delhi's Rodrigo Pinho.While the Aimen-led Delhi attack kept up the momentum, NEUFC attack, led by Alaaeddine Ajaraie and Ethyan Gonzalez, began beating their markers and growing into the game.It was a repeat of the earlier proceedings, this time to the disappointment of NEUFC, as a brilliant strike from the left edge of the box by Moroccan talisman Ajaraie was deemed offside moments after the celebration had begun in the stands.While NEUFC had the better chances towards the end of the game, through Ajaraie, Gonzalez and Jithin MS, Hnamte almost got his goal in the first minute of stoppage time. However, none of them were good enough to change the outcome, as the match stayed level until the final whistle.
Article Summary: NorthEast United FC and SC Delhi played out an exciting 1-1 draw on Indian Super League ’s debut in the football-loving state. NEUFC stayed in third spot, with 12 points from seven matches, while SC Delhi were still a rung below with nine points from their seven games.

Article Title: 'Lot of runs here': Forget the seamer-friendly reputation, New Zealand pacer says Hagley Oval pitch can flatten out
Article Text:
​New Zealand's Henry Nicholls, center, bats against India during the first day of the first cricket test match in Wellington, New Zealand.

New Zealand pacer Matt Henry has cautioned against reading too much into Hagley Oval's reputation as a seamer-friendly venue ahead of the second Test against India, which begins in Christchurch on Friday. The warning comes after the opening Test in Wellington turned into a batting-dominated contest despite expectations of assistance for fast bowlers.Only 24 wickets fell across five days in the drawn first Test, with India scoring 720 in their second innings, their highest total overseas. India captain Shubman Gill had expressed his disappointment with the pitch after the teams shook hands with more than 15 overs remaining on the final day.Henry, who has enjoyed success at Hagley Oval, said New Zealand would wait to see how the surface behaves rather than make plans based on its reputation."I think every game's different, every surface you play on is slightly different as well. And I think there's been a lot of runs scored here of late as well," Henry said at a press conference on Wednesday."So for us, it's probably not to get carried away with what it could be and trying to read pitches.It's a pretty fine art to do that."There is reason for New Zealand to be cautious about the conditions. India A and New Zealand A played a four-day match at the venue earlier this month, which also ended in a draw after both teams scored heavily.New Zealand A made 424 in their first innings, with Matt Boyle scoring 110, in reply to India A's 346, which included Dhruv Jurel's 105. India A then scored 282 for two in their second innings, with Yashasvi Jaiswal unbeaten on 155, as the pitch became easier for batting.Henry acknowledged that Hagley Oval has traditionally offered help to fast bowlers, particularly through bounce and carry. However, he said batting conditions can improve as a match progresses."I think traditionally here in New Zealand, the wickets when there's grass on them tend to get better and better, and it's been the same here. It's a good batting venue. Obviously, when there's bounce involved, it's good for the bowler, but from a batting point of view you can score runs quickly as well," he said.The 34-year-old also said batters would need to rely on their defence during difficult periods before looking to score freely."There's moments where you probably have to rely on your defence a little bit, but when you get through those periods, you really can put bowlers under pressure because, like you said, when it flattens out, your margins become pretty small as a bowler."Henry added that playing at home gives New Zealand a degree of familiarity with the ground, though the team would still have to assess the conditions during the match."It's always nice when you're at home and it is a ground you've played a lot of cricket at, so you probably have that element of comfort. You kind of know the ground well and whatnot."But yeah, it's been a great place to play cricket in the past, somewhere I love to play cricket."
Article Summary: New Zealand pacer Matt Henry has cautioned against reading too much into Hagley Oval's reputation as a seamer-friendly venue. The warning comes after the opening Test in Wellington turned into a batting-dominated contest. Henry said New Zealand would wait to see how the surface behaves rather than make plans based on its reputation.

Article Title: AFC Champions League: Jeakson’s late strike fuels East Bengal’s knockout hopes
Article Text:
Jeakson Singh (second from right) scores East Bengal’s winner against Al-Hussein at Salt Lake Stadium.

KOLKATA: Sometimes, football defies logic. East Bengal FC’s historic 1-0 win against Jordanian champions Al-Hussein SC in the reverse fixture of their AFC Champions League Two clash here on Tuesday — a first by an Indian club since the continent’s second-tier club tournament was rebranded in 2024 — was one such moment.After living on the edge for most of the contest and getting rescued by the woodwork four times, East Bengal somehow flipped the script. They earned a corner in the 87th minute — their first in the second session — and Bashim Rashid whipped in a well-measured delivery towards the first post. David Lalhlansanga deftly placed the ball in front of Jeakson Singh, who fired home.After two draws and two losses, East Bengal kept their hopes of advancing to the round of 16 alive with this win. They will travel to face Group D leaders Al Shorta of Iraq on Dec. 8. Only the top two from each group will make the knockouts.
Article Summary: East Bengal FC beat Jordanian champions Al-Hussein SC 1-0. Jeakson Singh scored the winner in the 87th minute at Salt Lake Stadium. It was the first AFC Champions League Two win by an Indian club since the continent’s second-tier club tournament was rebranded in 2024.

Article Title: ‘ICC, boards need to step in’: Harbhajan Singh on India-Pakistan cricket skirmishes
Article Text:
Harbhajan Singh has joined the chorus of those voicing their concern at the deteriorating player behaviour during India-Pakistan clashes.

'Have some patience with Team India'

MUMBAI: The last couple of India-Pakistan cricket contests, while they've provided plenty of excitement, have also seen ugly scenes of skirmishes between the players. On November 14, India's Under-19 players had a go at their Pakistani counterparts, celebrating wildly and overenthusiastically after pipping their arch-rivals by one wicket in a thrilling Under-19 Asia Cup final at Al Amerat in Oman. On November 22 (Sunday) in Doha, players of both India A and Pakistan A (Pakistani Shaheens) exchanged verbal volleys with each other, with India A pacer Harshit Rana involved in heated altercations with the Pakistan players during their Asia Cup Rising Stars match in Doha, which Pakistan A won by 48 runs.After the ugly scenes witnessed in the Asia Cup Under-19 final, former India skipper Dilip Vengsarkar had told TOI about the need for the BCCI to educate young cricketers at the BCCI's Centre of Excellence about behaving well on the field while playing for India at any level. India's off-spin great Harbhajan Singh has joined the chorus of those voicing their concern at the deteriorating player behaviour during these clashes and has urged the game's authorities — the International Cricket Council and the BCCI — to "step in" to check the trend of players from both countries getting carried away in Indo-Pak cricket matches."Somewhere down the line, the ICC needs to step in. I think it is just getting a bit too much with the reactions. First, Pakistan's boys did it (after beating India Under-19s in the league stage). Then the Indians won and did it. And then yesterday too, whatever happened was not right. If you look at sport as a sport, then it will be far better. See, some amount of chit chat happens, and has been happening for a long time. That should happen also.The game needs a bit of masala (spice) like that. However, it should not reach a point where you feel it is shameful. So, somewhere down the line, I think that the ICC and the respective boards need to put their foot forward and say, 'this is not done.' 'You try hard on the field to win the match for your team, try your best, but after the match, those reactions, I don't think are the right ones. Both from our side and their side," Harbhajan told reporters at an event at the BPGC Golf Course here on Tuesday.Asked specifically about Rana's on-field clashes with Pakistan's players, Harbhajan quipped, "I don't think that should happen. I think it is not setting the right example for the generation coming up."While he wasn't critical of India's bowlers' inability to take New Zealand's eight remaining wickets on the final day of the first Test at Wellington, which ended in a draw on Monday, calling the pitch "really flat," Harbhajan, who took 417 wickets in 103 Tests (1998-2015), wasn't entirely convinced about India's decision to shake hands with their Kiwi counterparts even with 15 overs left to be bowled in the last session of the match, and felt that they could have continued bowling. "I thought the pitch was dry and very flat. It's okay. Pitches in Australia and New Zealand tend to be really flat, at times.“I think a lot has been talked about in this game. There were 15 overs left and they declared the game (a draw) before. Yes, you could have tried. You never know. Things move very fast in cricket. But somewhere down the line, you have to be honest with yourself, as a captain and management, whether it was the right decision on that pitch or in that scenario. I think that a lot of thought would have gone into that decision. But if I was part of the management, I would have liked to bowl another 15 overs and give it a try. And let's see. You never know,” Harbhajan said.Recalling how former Australia captain Michael Clarke, with his part-time left-arm spin, had bowled Australia to a win against India in the closing minutes of the controversial Sydney Test in January 2008, taking three for five in 1.5 overs, the former tweaker said, "After everyone else had bowled, Australia introduced Clarke just two overs before (the close of the Test). And nothing was happening. Suddenly he came and he took those two important wickets and they ended up winning that match. So, cricket is a very funny game. Anything can happen."Citing the fighting attitude of his former India spin-bowling partner and ex-India captain Anil Kumble, Harbhajan said, "I have always been a fan of Anil Bhai. And I still say that his attitude was that you have to fight till the last ball. Whether you are bowling or batting or in the field, you have to fight till the last ball. So 90 balls is a lot. I think we should have tried in those 90 balls (to get the remaining five Kiwi wickets). You never know. Maybe the result will come in your favour."Harbhajan defended off-spinner Washington Sundar, who took one for 65 in 35 overs as the Kiwis secured a draw in the first Test. "It's very easy for all of us to pinpoint an individual and say he could have done this or he could have done that. I will put myself in his position. He tried his best. He is young. He is learning. And of course, the more he plays, the more he will learn about these situations. Next time, if he is in such a situation, I am sure he will be able to perform better. So, let's not pinpoint an individual. You win with 11, you lose with 11 and you throw with 11. He must have tried. If it was me, I would have tried as well. So, give him some time. I am sure he will learn and he will get better," Harbhajan stressed.Critics have panned India's inability to close out Test wins in their last two games by taking wickets on the fifth and final day — it happened against Sri Lanka in Colombo in August, and then against New Zealand on the final day of the first Test at Wellington. Harbhajan, though, isn't perturbed and urged fans to "have some patience with the Indian team.""That will happen (closing out Test wins). This is the same team that won in England (India drew the Test series 2-2 last summer in England). Have some patience with the team. We have a trend here. If you don't get a result that we want from the Indian team, then we go after it. Give them a break. They need to 'breathe out' as well. They are on the road continuously. So, give them some break. I'm sure that they'll get the right results for Team India. "Would it have made a difference if Ravindra Jadeja and Mohammed Siraj had played? "Time will tell. You say, what would have happened if Kapil paaji had played? I can't say much about what would have happened. But if he would have played, we would have talked about it. I can't really predict what would have happened if he would have played. If I would have known, I would have called Gautam and asked him to play," Harbhajan retorted.Talking about the ongoing 'Sandpaper-gate' controversy rearing its head in Australian cricket again, Harbhajan felt that it "wasn't a new thing" and that it showed that the Australian team sometimes received far more respect than they deserved."I don't think this is a new thing. This is a very old thing. Pakistan and India have been talking about this for a long time. That this is a reverse swing.We are making such a big thing about this. Australia was doing it before. England was doing it. South Africa was doing it. Wherever there is reverse swing, there must be something with the ball. People are doing it. How much they do it naturally, or the way they have done it with sandpaper, that is a little bad.Naturally, if you go to make the ball reverse, it takes some time to get the ball going. But if you make the ball reverse in the 10th over, then it is understood that there can be nothing but teasing."Australia is not as simple as they used to be. Their players are not as simple as they used to be. I have said this from day one, they should not be given so much respect. They should be given a lot of respect. They have also played the game. They have also done all these things. Now they have been caught or things have come out, they are saying that they did not know. It is not possible that you are living in one house, you are living in another house, you do not know who is living there. Everybody was part of it. I believe. If it is in the team, then it is a collective thing."
Article Summary: Harbhajan Singh has joined the chorus of those voicing their concern at the deteriorating player behaviour during India-Pakistan clashes. India's off-spin great has urged the game's authorities to "step in" to check the trend of players from both countries getting carried away in Indo-Pak cricket matches.

Article Title: BIMSTEC U23 Athletics Championships: Amid personal loss, Priya Sheoran hopes to make her mark
Article Text:
(From left) Bhartpreet Singh, Rahul Sarnaliya, Sadhna Ravi, Priya

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The past few months have tested Priya Sheoran in ways far beyond the athletics field.The Haryana discus thrower had been making frequent trips to hospital as her father Anup, a sub-inspector with Haryana Police and the man who inspired her to take up sports, had been unwell for several months. He passed away on Nov 10.Barely a fortnight later, Priya is set to step into the competition arena again, carrying both the grief of her loss and the hope of putting up a strong performance at the three-day inaugural BIMSTEC U23 Athletics Championships to be held at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar from Wednesday.“For the past four months, I had been going back and forth to the hospital with him. So, the preparation hasn’t been that good, but let’s hope for the best,” said Priya.The youngster, who has trained under celebrated discus thrower Seema Punia, won bronze at the U23 Asian Athletics Championships earlier this year, her first international medal.“It felt really good because it was my first international medal. This tournament is also being organised for the first time, so I’ll try to perform well here too and hopefully win a medal,” said the 22-year-old.Given what she has been through in recent months, Priya is trying not to burden herself with expectations.“I just want to put my best foot forward and give my best. I haven’t really thought about the result yet. I’ll go in with the mindset that I have to perform well,” she added.Priya will be among a 70-member Indian contingent looking to make an impression at the event.A little more than 200 athletes from six countries are expected to compete in the three-day event. With Thailand pulling out, athletes from Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar, Nepal and Sri Lanka will join hosts India in the competition.Among those attracting attention will also be 17-year-old sprinter Neil Samraj, who comes into the event on the back of a record-breaking season.Samraj broke the U18 national record in the 100m twice in a single day at the National Youth Athletics Championships in Ludhiana, eventually clocking 10.46s in the final. He lowered the mark further at the National Junior Athletics Championships in Chennai last month, running 10.45s. He also rewrote the U18 national record in the 200m in Chennai with a time of 21.03 seconds.Now, with an opportunity to test himself against athletes from the region, Samraj wants to see where he stands at the end of a long season.“Competing internationally will help me gain experience and prepare for many more international competitions where I will be up against athletes from different countries,” Samraj said in a social media post released by the Athletics Federation of India.“The plan is just to go hard because this is a very good opportunity to participate in a regional international competition. It will also help me understand where I stand and what kind of timings I can produce towards the end of the season.”For India’s young athletes, the championships provide another international opportunity at the end of a season that has witnessed several national records tumble. For Priya, however, simply returning to the throwing circle after a difficult few months will carry a significance of its own.
Article Summary: Priya Sheoran to compete at BIMSTEC U23 Athletics Championships in Bhubaneswar. Haryana discus thrower will be carrying the grief of her father's death. Priya won bronze at the U23 Asian Athletics Championships earlier this year.

Article Title: ILT20: Gulf Giants crush MI Emirates for second straight win as Shamar Joseph stars with the ball
Article Text:
Shamar Joseph celebrates for the Gulf Giants against the MI Emirates in the ILT20. (Creimas)

Dubai:

Brief scores

MI Emirates 91 in 19.3 overs

Gulf Giants 93/4 in 13.5 overs

Gulf Giants continued their winning start to the ILT20 Season 5, registering a six-wicket victory over MI Emirates at the Dubai International Stadium on Tuesday after bowling them out for just 91.ILT20 debutant Shamar Joseph and David Wiese claimed three wickets each as MI Emirates were dismissed in 19.3 overs for their lowest total in the league. The 91 was also the joint-second lowest score recorded in Dubai in ILT20 history.Shamar returned figures of 3/9, while Wiese finished with 3/19. Alzarri Joseph, Azmatullah Omarzai and Haider Razzaq picked up a wicket each as Gulf Giants kept MI Emirates in check throughout the innings.The chase was far from straightforward initially, with Gulf Giants losing Rahmanullah Gurbaz (0) and Liam Livingstone (1) inside the first two overs. Omarzai (6) and Dhruv Parashar (15) also fell, leaving the Giants at 50/4.However, Ibrahim Zadran and Heinrich Klaasen steadied the innings with an unbeaten 43-run partnership to take Gulf Giants home in 13.5 overs.Zadran finished on 50 not out from 35 balls, hitting five fours and a six, while Klaasen contributed 16 off 16 deliveries, including a four and a six.Earlier, MI Emirates suffered an early setback when Muhammad Waseem (4) was bowled by Omarzai in the opening over.Shamar then struck twice in the fourth over, removing Kusal Perera (6) and Sanjay Krishnamurthi (0), before dismissing Sherfane Rutherford (1) in the final over of the powerplay.MI Emirates were reduced to 22/4, with Shamar having conceded no runs until his fourth wicket.Nicholas Pooran attempted to revive the innings with Kieron Pollard, but their 29-run stand was broken by Wiese in the 12th over. Pooran departed for 23 off 34 balls, while Pollard was dismissed for 13 by Haider Razzaq in the following over.Rashid Khan (7), Romario Shepherd (13) and Jordan Thompson (3) offered little resistance as MI Emirates continued to lose wickets. Wiese removed Thompson in the 18th over before the innings ended at 91 in 19.3 overs.Player of the Match, Gulf Giants' Shamar Joseph said, "I thought it was simple. I saw Omarzai bowling and the ball was seaming and swinging. It's my debut here, and I'm feeling amazing about what I did. Our chances are good. You meet new people, and a lot of them have played around the world, which helps me. Getting information on the conditions is important."MI Emirates skipper Kieron Pollard said, "We lost a couple of wickets in clusters. You practice for scenarios and conditions, so you don't use pitches as an excuse. I told the bowlers not to look for magic balls. I fielded at short leg numerous times just to try and put pressure on the opponents.There's no need to dissect it much, as it was tough for both sides' batters."(Nicholas Pooran 23, Kieron Pollard 13, Romario Shepherd 13, Shamar Joseph 3 for 9, David Wiese 3 for 19)(Ibrahim Zadran 50*, Heinrich Klaasen 16*, Dhruv Parashar 15, Jordan Thompson 2 for 27, Fazalhaq Farooqi 1 for 21)
Article Summary: ILT20 debutant Shamar Joseph and David Wiese claimed three wickets each as MI Emirates were dismissed in 19.3 overs for their lowest total in the league. Ibrahim Zadran and Heinrich Klaasen steadied the innings with an unbeaten 43-run partnership.

The Indian Street Premier League (ISPL) will move to Goa for its fourth season, with the tennis-ball T10 tournament scheduled to run from December 6, 2026, to January 3, 2027. Eight franchises will compete in 44 matches at the 1919 Sportz Cricket Stadium in Verna.Defending champions Chennai Singams will open the season against last year's runners-up Tiigers of Kolkata on December 6, setting up a rematch of the Season 3 final. Chennai Singams are co-owned by Suriya and Rajdip Gupta, while Tiigers of Kolkata are co-owned by Saif Ali Khan, Kareena Kapoor Khan and Aksha Kamboj.The opening day's fixture will be followed by Majhi Mumbai taking on Ahmedabad Lions on December 4. Srinagar Ke Veer will face Bengaluru Strikers, while Falcon Risers Hyderabad take on Delhi Superheros in the first double-header of the season.The league stage will conclude on December 28, followed by Qualifier 1 on December 29, the Eliminator on December 30 and Qualifier 2 on January 2. The final is scheduled for January 3, 2027.Single-header matches will begin at 8pm, while double-header days will start at 5:30pm.The move to Goa comes as the league looks to expand its reach and strengthen its grassroots talent pathway. Across its first three editions, ISPL has provided a platform for aspiring cricketers from different parts of the country to showcase their abilities in the tennis-ball format.The Season 4 auction also reflected the league's growing commercial footprint, with the eight franchises collectively spending more than ₹10.40 crore.ISPL League Commissioner Suraj Samat said Goa's tourist season offered an opportunity to bring sport and tourism together while continuing to develop the league's talent pool.“Goa offers a fantastic setting for ISPL Season 4, with the schedule also coinciding with the state’s peak tourist season. This presents a natural opportunity for the league to flourish at the intersection of sport and tourism,” Samat said.The league has also revised its player selection process, removing simulation matches and introducing a data-driven system based on performances in local tournaments across the country. The top 500 performers will qualify for the auction pool through points accumulated in these competitions, alongside the top 50 contracted players.The revised process is intended to reduce human intervention and provide a performance-based route for grassroots players to enter the league.
Article Summary: ISPL Season 4 will begin on December 6, 2026 and will be played in Goa. All matches are played in the Indian Super League (ISL) The finals will be held on January 3, 2027. The final will take place at the Maracana in Mumbai.

Article Title: Imesha Dulani, Sathya Sandeepani star as Sri Lanka beat Ireland to win Women's Emerging Nations Trophy
Article Text:
Sri Lanka defeated Ireland by six wickets to win the ICC Women’s Emerging Nations Trophy 2026 (Image: IANS)

Sri Lanka's bowlers bundle out Ireland for 96

Imesha Dulani guides Sri Lanka to title

Brief Scores

Ireland Women: 96 all out in 19.3 overs (Alana Dalzell 24, Louise Little 15; Sathya Sandeepani 4/13) lost to Sri Lanka Women: 99/4 in 12.4 overs (Imesha Dulani 44*, Sanjana Kavindi 25; Kia McCartney 2/16, Cara Murray 2/38) by six wickets.

Sri Lanka produced a commanding all-round performance to defeat Ireland by six wickets and clinch the ICC Women's Emerging Nations Trophy 2026 on Wednesday. Imesha Dulani starred with an unbeaten 44 as Sri Lanka comfortably chased down the 97-run target in just 12.4 overs in the final at the Karwan Sports Club.The victory marked Sri Lanka's first title in the tournament's history, succeeding Thailand, who won the inaugural edition in 2025.After opting to bat first, Ireland endured a disastrous start, losing captain Gaby Lewis in the opening over at 5/1. The early setback soon turned into a collapse as they slipped to 10/2 before struggling to recover. Sri Lanka's disciplined bowling attack kept the pressure firmly on Ireland, reducing them to 54/6 inside 12 overs.Alana Dalzell emerged as Ireland's top scorer with 24 off 25 deliveries, while Louise Little contributed 15 off 17 balls. Georgina Dempsey also chipped in with 13, but Ireland failed to build meaningful partnerships and were eventually bowled out for 96 in 19.3 overs.Sathya Sandeepani was the standout performer with the ball, claiming four wickets for just 13 runs in her four overs. Kavisha Dilhari, Sugandika Kumari, Nimasha Meepage and Chethana Vimukthi picked up a wicket apiece, while two run-outs further dented Ireland's innings.Chasing 97, Sri Lanka made an aggressive start but suffered a brief setback after Sanjana Kavindi departed for 25 off 22 balls. Captain Harshitha Samarawickrama was dismissed for a golden duck on the following delivery, leaving Sri Lanka at 35/2.Ireland attempted to stage a comeback through Kia McCartney and Cara Murray, who picked up two wickets each to reduce Sri Lanka to 69/4 in the ninth over.However, Dulani held her nerve and ensured there were no further hiccups. She remained unbeaten on 44, while Dilhari provided valuable support with an unbeaten 16 off just 10 deliveries.The pair stitched together an unbroken 30-run partnership to take Sri Lanka to 99/4 in 12.4 overs, sealing a convincing six-wicket victory and the championship trophy.
Article Summary: Sri Lanka defeated Ireland by six wickets to win the ICC Women’s Emerging Nations Trophy 2026. Imesha Dulani starred with an unbeaten 44 as Sri Lanka comfortably chased down the 97-run target in just 12.4 overs.

NEW DELHI: New Zealand bowling coach Jacob Oram has been left impressed by the extraordinary rise of teenage batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, but he has a request for the 15-year-old: save his most destructive innings for someone else.Sooryavanshi has taken the cricketing world by storm with his astonishing exploits, most recently smashing a breathtaking 204 off just 53 balls in a List A match on Tuesday. His innings, which accounted for 204 of India A's 254 runs, powered the side to a seven-wicket victory in a chase of 250 in just 14.2 overs, making the contest look more like a video game than a traditional 50-over match.The knock has also reignited the debate over the relevance of ODI cricket amid the growing popularity of T20s. However, Oram believes it is premature to put the responsibility of saving the format on the shoulders of a teenager."It's a bit cool to call a 15-year-old the saviour. Let's see how it pans out. I understand the public love their T20 cricket and the purists love Test cricket, but I still believe there's a place for 50-over cricket," Oram told PTI.The former New Zealand all-rounder, however, had no reservations about acknowledging the youngster's extraordinary talent."He's (Sooryavanshi) exciting, he's entertaining, and the more of those players involved in cricket, the better it is for the product. I just hope he doesn't get a 50-ball double hundred when we have to bowl against him," he said.Oram also recalled the teenager's explosive batting against New Zealand in the Wellington T20I, where he scored 45 off just 19 balls."He got one score against us, did he not? (45 in 19 balls in the Wellington T20I) and you could see some glimpses of it. I have seen enough of him on TV in the IPL and elsewhere. This guy is amazing, whatever he is, 15 or 16?. Even if he was 25 or 26, like let us say 10 years older, the age is not a factor; it is about how good he is. A 50-ball 200 is crazy, right? You know, and you sort of wonder where you go from there," Oram told ANI."I have said, though, I just hope it is not against us, and we have to, every time we play him, we have got to make sure we are on our game or else that sort of stuff could happen because he is a talent," he added.Sooryavanshi's numbers underline why opposition bowling attacks are already wary of him. In 16 List A appearances, he has accumulated 805 runs at an average of 50.31 and a strike rate of over 193, including two centuries and two half-centuries. He has also smashed 63 sixes in 16 innings.His exploits in Youth ODIs have been equally remarkable. Representing India Under-19, he has scored 1,412 runs in 25 innings at an average of 56.48 and a strike rate of 165.72, with four centuries and seven fifties. His best score is 175, which came against England in the Under-19 World Cup final earlier this year.In 10 T20Is for India, the left-hander has already scored 295 runs at a strike rate of over 185, including two half-centuries and a highest score of 81.

Article Title: Karnataka lost in transition: R Smaran & co’s SMAT campaign ends prematurely in chaos
Article Text:
Karnataka's Abhinav Manohar. (PTI File Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Lack of consistency, a chaotic campaign and an early exit sum up Karnataka’s Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy T20 season. Although they laboured to a four-wicket win over Rajasthan in Mumbai on Tuesday, the mathematical hope R Smaran and his team clung to evaporated. With Baroda having sealed qualification from Group A, the result had no bearing on Karnataka’s fate. The second spot will be decided by the outcome of the final league encounter between Rajasthan and Bengal.This was Karnataka’s fourth consecutive league-phase exit in the tournament. In the six matches they have played so far, the former champions have hardly looked like contenders. Instead, they have resembled a team caught in a cycle of experimentation. Karnataka have fielded 16 players, with only three — Smaran, Manvanth Kumar and Pravin Dubey — featuring in all six matches.The decision to recall Manish Pandey yielded little, while the persistence with an under-fire Abhinav Manohar did not pay dividends either. The musical chairs at the top of the order only added to the uncertainty, resulting in below-par returns. Tellingly, Karnataka have managed just three half-centuries, with seasoned campaigner Karun Nair accounting for two and Smaran the other.Around 14 players across teams have scored at a strike rate of over 200, but among Karnataka’s top and middle-order batters, Luvnith Sisodia has the best strike rate at 154. Their struggles were also reflected in the team’s totals. Karnataka’s highest score while batting first was 184 in the tournament opener against Bengal, while their lowest was a dismal 95 against Chandigarh.Bowling has also proved to be a major weakness. As many as 12 players have been tried with the ball, but barring Manvanth Kumar, the lone bright spark with 91 runs and 10 wickets, the returns have been largely underwhelming. Abhilash Shetty and Ritesh Bhatkal showed promise in patches, but the rest failed to make a telling impact.It has been one of those rare Karnataka campaigns where the overriding expectation was not a stirring performance, but when the team would implode next.With their campaign ending prematurely, head coach R Vinay Kumar and the selectors have time to take stock of what went wrong, particularly some of the questionable decisions that disrupted the team’s balance. The focus will now shift to the Vijay Hazare Trophy, where Karnataka will hope to start afresh.If this is a team in transition, it is clear that Karnataka are yet to find their way through it.
Article Summary: Karnataka's fourth consecutive league-phase exit in the tournament. Former champions have hardly looked like contenders. Karnataka have fielded 16 players, with only three featuring in all six matches. The decision to recall Manish Pandey yielded little.

Article Title: Best ever! From 14 medals to 114: How India achieved more with fewer athletes at the Asian Para Games
Article Text:
Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

From 14 medals to 114: India's remarkable rise

India's Asian Para Games record

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Smaller contingent, bigger return

Hangzhou vs Aichi-Nagoya

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Athletics powers India's medal surge

India's leading medal-winning sports in Asian Para Games 2026

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Multiple medallists underline India's depth

Paralympic progress provides the wider context

Fourth place sets a new benchmark

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

From 14 medals in 2010 to 114 in 2026, India’s remarkable rise continued in Aichi-Nagoya as a smaller contingent surpassed its previous best, achieved 30 gold medals and secured its highest-ever finish at the continental para-sport showpiece.India’s campaign at the Asian Para Games 2026 was a triumph that few would have predicted when the size of the contingent became known. With just 167 athletes travelling to Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the prospect of repeating the 100-plus medal haul achieved at Hangzhou in 2023 appeared ambitious. The previous edition had seen India send more than 300 athletes to the competition, returning with a record 108 medals after subsequent revisions to the original tally.But the Indian contingent defied expectations, producing an even bigger return with significantly fewer athletes. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place, both the highest medal tally and the best finish in the country's history at the event.The numbers tell a compelling story of progress. India improved its medal tally for the fifth consecutive edition, added to its gold-medal record and finished ahead of South Korea, which had threatened to challenge its position in the final standings.More than the record itself, the achievement highlighted how far India's para-sport movement has travelled in 16 years — from a modest 14-medal return at the inaugural edition in 2010 to a fourth-place finish among Asia's leading para-sport nations.India's progress at the Asian Para Games has been steady, with each edition bringing a new high in the overall medal tally.At Guangzhou in 2010, India won 14 medals — one gold, four silver and nine bronze — to finish 15th. The 2014 edition in Incheon brought a substantial improvement, with the country collecting 33 medals, including three gold, but remaining 15th in the standings.The breakthrough arrived at Jakarta in 2018. India's medal tally rose to 72, comprising 15 gold, 24 silver and 33 bronze, while its position improved to ninth.Hangzhou in 2023 marked another major leap. India crossed the 100-medal barrier for the first time, initially returning with 111 medals before the tally was revised to 108 following a doping-related disqualification and a medal reallocation. The revised haul comprised 27 gold, 32 silver and 49 bronze, with India eventually classified sixth.Aichi-Nagoya extended that upward trajectory. India added six medals to its revised Hangzhou total, increased its gold-medal count from 27 to 30 and climbed two places to fourth.The numbers at a glance: India's medal tally increased more than eightfold between 2010 and 2026. Its gold-medal count grew from one to 30, while its position improved from 15th to fourth.The rise has not been limited to the overall tally. India has improved its standing in three successive editions since 2014, moving from 15th to ninth, then sixth and now fourth. The 2026 result represents the culmination of a sustained upward trend rather than an isolated breakthrough.The most striking feature of India's latest performance was the efficiency with which its athletes converted participation into medals.India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi-Nagoya. That was considerably fewer than the 309 athletes listed for the Hangzhou campaign in 2023, yet the team surpassed its previous best by six medals.The comparison is revealing. India sent approximately 46 per cent fewer athletes than it did to Hangzhou, but its medal tally increased by nearly six per cent. The gold-medal count rose by three, the silver tally by three, and the bronze count remained unchanged.On a simple medals-per-athlete measure, India's return increased from approximately 0.35 medals per athlete in Hangzhou to 0.68 in Aichi-Nagoya. This is an aggregate comparison, not an individual success rate, since athletes can win multiple medals and the number of events and opportunities varies across sports.Nevertheless, the figures underline the scale of the achievement. A smaller squad did not merely match the previous edition's success; it established a new benchmark for Indian para-sport.Para-athletics was the backbone of India's campaign, delivering 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. That represented nearly 57 per cent of the country's overall tally and made athletics the single biggest contributor to India's fourth-place finish.Para-badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze. Together, athletics and badminton accounted for 81 medals, more than 70 per cent of India's total.Swimming contributed 11 medals, comprising three silver and eight bronze. Archery added six medals, including three gold and three silver, while shooting produced five, with two gold, two silver and one bronze.Athletics' contribution also illustrates how India's progress has accelerated. At Hangzhou, para-athletics produced 52 medals, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 19 bronze. In Aichi-Nagoya, the discipline's haul rose to 65, with six additional gold medals.Badminton's contribution was different. India won 21 medals in the sport at Hangzhou, including four gold, but finished with 16 in 2026. Instead, the substantial gains in athletics and the contributions from other sports helped compensate for the decline in badminton medals.That distinction matters: the record haul reflects both the strength of India's established medal-winning disciplines and the need to broaden its success across events in future editions.India's record was supported by athletes who delivered more than once during the competition. A total of 26 Indian athletes won multiple medals, while six athletes collected multiple gold medals, demonstrating the importance of individual excellence in a campaign involving 11 sports.Archer Sheetal Devi was among the standout performers, winning two gold medals and a silver. Her two golds came in the mixed compound and individual compound events, while the silver added to her three-medal haul.Athletics provided several other multiple gold medallists. Dilip Gavit, Nishad Kumar, Pranav Soorma and Simran Sharma each won two gold medals, while shooting contributed through Mona Agarwal, who also secured two golds.Four athletes finished with three medals apiece: Sheetal Devi in archery, Thulasimathi Murugesan in badminton, Ravi Budigina in swimming and Himanshu Nandal in swimming. Their performances illustrated how athletes winning across multiple events can make a significant difference to a country's final tally.The figures also invite comparison with Hangzhou, where 25 Indian athletes won multiple medals. The increase to 26 in 2026 was modest, but the overall tally improved despite a much smaller contingent. The result points to a campaign in which medal-winning performances were concentrated among a relatively small squad.India's rise at the Asian Para Games has coincided with a significant improvement at the Paralympics, strengthening the country's standing in international para-sport.At Rio 2016, India won four medals and finished 43rd. Tokyo 2020 marked a breakthrough, with 19 medals — five gold, eight silver and six bronze — lifting India to 24th. At Paris 2024, India recorded its best Paralympic haul of 29 medals, comprising seven gold, nine silver and 13 bronze, to finish 18th.The progression at the Paralympics mirrors the broader trend at the Asian Para Games: larger medal returns, more gold medals and improvements in the standings.India's able-bodied contingent had also finished fourth at the 2026 Asian Games, although its 85-medal tally was below the 106 medals achieved at Hangzhou in 2023. The para contingent's performance offered a contrasting story of growth, with its medal count rising and its position improving.China dominated Aichi-Nagoya, finishing with 435 medals, including 207 gold. Hosts Japan were second with 186 medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 145. India placed fourth with 114, ahead of South Korea, which collected 100 medals, including 29 gold.India's final position was not guaranteed until the closing stages. South Korea remained within reach, but its final-day return of one gold and two silver left it one gold behind India. The Indian contingent held on to fourth place with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze.The gap to third-placed Uzbekistan shows that further progress will require India to expand its medal-winning strength across disciplines. Yet the immediate achievement is significant: India has moved from 15th at the first two editions to fourth, while increasing its tally at every successive Games.The challenge now is to sustain that momentum, build a deeper pool of competitive athletes and reduce dependence on a handful of disciplines.For a contingent of just 167 athletes, 114 medals represent more than a record. They mark the latest step in a 16-year transformation of Indian para-sport — one that began with 14 medals in Guangzhou and has now culminated in a historic fourth-place finish in Aichi-Nagoya.
Article Summary: India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi- Nagoya. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place. It is the best finish in the country's history at the event.
